t.5.35.1: Having heard his words, Sītā, whose face was like the full moon, spoke these words to Hanūmān, words consonant with dharma and artha.
t.5.35.2: What you have told me, O monkey, is nectar mixed with poison: that Rāma thinks of nothing else, and that he is wholly given over to grief.
t.5.35.3: Whether in vast prosperity or in most terrible calamity, Fate binds a man as if with a rope and drags him along.
t.5.35.5: When will Rāghava reach the far shore of this grief, like a man whose boat is wrecked, swimming exhausted in the ocean?
t.5.35.4: Surely fate is inescapable for living beings, O best of monkeys. See how Saumitri, Rāma and I are confounded by misfortunes.
t.5.35.6: Having brought destruction upon the Rākṣasas and slain Rāvaṇa, having uprooted Laṅkā, when will my husband see me?
t.5.35.7: He should be told, "Make haste!" For only so long as this period of one year is not yet complete will my life endure.
t.5.35.8: The tenth month is now passing, O monkey, and only two remain of the time limit that the cruel Rāvaṇa set for me.
t.5.35.9: And though he was earnestly entreated by his brother Vibhīṣaṇa to return me, he does not set his mind to that.
t.5.35.11: O monkey, the eldest daughter of Vibhīṣaṇa, a maiden named Analā, sent by her mother herself, told me this.
t.5.35.10: Returning me does not please Rāvaṇa, for Death seeks out Rāvaṇa in battle, he who has fallen under the sway of Time.
t.5.35.12: There is a rākṣasa named Avindhya, foremost among the rākṣasas, intelligent and learned, steadfast, virtuous and aged, and highly esteemed by Rāvaṇa.
t.5.35.13: He warned him of the destruction of the rākṣasas that was approaching from Rāma, yet that evil-minded one does not listen even to his beneficial words.
t.5.35.14: O best of monkeys, tell him this: "My husband will swiftly come to me, for my inner self is pure, and in him there are many virtues."
t.5.35.15: Zeal, manliness, strength of spirit, compassion, gratitude, valor and majesty are all present in Rāghava, O monkey.
t.5.35.16: He who slew fourteen thousand rākṣasas in Janasthāna without his brother, what enemy would not tremble before him?
t.5.35.17: That bull among men cannot be weighed down by misfortunes. I know his might, as Pulomajā knows the might of Śakra.
t.5.35.18: O monkey, the heroic sun that is Rāma, whose rays are a net of arrows, will dry up the water that is made of the enemy rākṣasas.
t.5.35.19: To her, who was speaking thus about Rāma, emaciated with grief, her face filled with tears, the monkey Hanumān spoke.
t.5.35.20: As soon as he hears my words, Rāghava will come swiftly, leading a mighty army teeming with hosts of monkeys and bears.
t.5.35.22: Placing you upon my back, I shall cross the ocean, for I have the strength to carry even Laṅkā itself together with Rāvaṇa.
t.5.35.21: Or rather, this very day I shall free that lady from the rākṣasa and from this sorrow; climb onto my back, O blameless one.
t.5.35.23: O Maithilī, this very day I shall bring you to Rāghava, who stays on Mount Prasravaṇa, just as fire carries the offered oblation to Śakra.
t.5.35.24: This very day, O Vaidehī, you will see Rāghava together with Lakṣmaṇa, firmly resolved and fully prepared, like Viṣṇu set upon the slaying of the Daityas.
t.5.35.25: You shall see that mighty one dwelling in the hermitage, his ardor kindled by the sight of you, like Puraṃdara seated upon the head of the king of elephants.
t.5.35.26: Climb upon my back, O queen; do not hesitate, O lovely one. Seek union with Rāma, as Rohiṇī with the moon.
t.5.35.28: For, O lady, as I set out from here carrying you away, all the dwellers of Laṅkā together will not be able to follow my course.
t.5.35.27: Climbing onto my back, cross the great ocean of the sky, as though conversing with the Moon, like Suvarcalā with the Sun.
t.5.35.29: Just as I have come here, so too, without doubt, shall I go, lifting you up into the sky; behold, Vaidehī!
t.5.35.30: But Maithilī, having heard the wondrous words from the best of monkeys, her whole body thrilled with joy and amazement, then spoke to Hanumān.
t.5.35.31: Hanumān, how can you wish to carry me over so long a road? That, I think, is surely just your monkey nature, O leader of the monkey troops.
t.5.35.32: Or how, with so small a body, do you wish to carry me from here into the presence of my husband, the lord of men, O bull among monkeys?
t.5.35.33: Having heard Sītā's words, the illustrious Hanumān, son of the Wind-god, thought that a fresh humiliation had been inflicted upon him.
t.5.35.35: Having thus reflected, Hanumān, the best of monkeys and crusher of foes, then revealed his own true form to Vaidehī.
t.5.35.34: The dark-eyed lady does not know my strength or my might; therefore let Vaidehī behold the form that I can assume at will.
t.5.35.36: Then that wise bull among monkeys leapt down from that tree and began to increase his size, in order to win Sītā's trust.
t.5.35.37: Resembling Mount Meru or Mandara, the bull among monkeys shone with the radiance of a blazing fire, and he stood before Sītā.
t.5.35.38: The monkey, resembling a mountain, copper-faced and mighty, terrible, with fangs and claws like thunderbolts, spoke these words to Vaidehī.
t.5.35.40: Therefore let your mind be made steady; enough of doubt, O queen. O Vaidehī, free Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa, from sorrow.
t.5.35.39: I have the strength to carry away this very Laṅkā, with its mountains and forest regions, its watchtowers, ramparts and gateways, together with its lord as well.
t.5.35.41: Seeing him, resembling a mountain, the daughter of Janaka, whose eyes were large like lotus petals, spoke to the true-born son of Māruta.
t.5.35.42: O great monkey, I know your courage and your strength, and your speed, which is like that of the wind; and your splendor is wondrous, like fire.
t.5.35.43: And how could any other ordinary being come to this land on the far shore of the immeasurable ocean, O bull among vānaras?
t.5.35.44: I know your power in going, and also in carrying me away. Yet, having quickly and carefully deliberated, one must certainly secure here the accomplishment of one's own purpose.
t.5.35.46: For as you speed swiftly through the sky high above the ocean, I, clinging to you, might fall from your back out of fear.
t.5.35.45: But it is not fitting for me to go with you, O best of monkeys, for the speed of you, whose speed equals the speed of the wind, would make me faint.
t.5.35.47: And having fallen into the ocean teeming with whales, crocodiles and fishes, I would quickly, helpless, become the choicest food for the sea-creatures.
t.5.35.49: But seeing me being carried away, the rākṣasas of terrible valor, commanded by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa, would follow in pursuit.
t.5.35.48: Nor shall I be able to go with you, O destroyer of enemies; suspicion would undoubtedly fall on you as well, as one travelling in the company of a woman.
t.5.35.50: Surrounded by those heroes bearing spears and maces in their hands, you, O hero, encumbered with me, a woman in your charge, would fall into grave peril.
t.5.35.51: Many armed rākṣasas will be in the sky, while you are unarmed; how will you be able to fight them and protect me as well?
t.5.35.52: Then, while you were fighting with those rākṣasas of cruel deeds, I, stricken with fear, might fall from your back, O best of monkeys.
t.5.35.53: Or else, O best of monkeys, the terrible rākṣasas, huge and mighty, might somehow overcome you in battle.
t.5.35.54: Or else, while you are fighting with your attention turned away, I might fall, and the wicked rākṣasas would seize me as I fell and carry me off.
t.5.35.55: They might snatch me from your hands, or else they might even slay me, for in battle victory and defeat are seen to be uncertain.
t.5.35.56: Or I might perish, menaced by the rākṣasas, and then, O best of monkeys, your effort would be fruitless indeed.
t.5.35.57: Granted, you too are fully capable of slaying all the rākṣasas; but the glory of Rāghava would be diminished if the rākṣasas were struck down by you.
t.5.35.58: Or else the Rākṣasas, seizing me, might place me in some hidden spot where neither those monkeys nor even Rāghava could find me.
t.5.35.59: This undertaking of yours on my behalf is therefore pointless, for there is great merit in Rāma's coming here together with you.
t.5.35.61: Those two, despairing on my account and wasted by grief and anguish, will give up their hold on life together with all the bears and monkeys.
t.5.35.60: On me depends the life of the great-souled Rāghava and of his brothers, O mighty-armed one, and of you, and of the royal house.
t.5.35.62: Placing devotion to my husband foremost, O monkey, I would not wish to touch with my foot the body of anyone other than Rāma, O best of monkeys.
t.5.35.63: That I came into contact with Rāvaṇa's body was by force; powerless, what could I do, a chaste woman without a protector and helpless?
t.5.35.64: If Rāma were to slay Daśagrīva here together with his rākṣasas and then take me from this place and go, that would be worthy of him.
t.5.35.65: Indeed, I have both heard of and witnessed the valorous deeds of that great-souled one, the crusher of foes in battle; neither gods nor gandharvas, serpents nor rākṣasas are equal to Rāma in combat.
t.5.35.66: Having beheld in battle that Rāghava, mighty in strength, wielding his wondrous bow, equal in prowess to Vāsava, together with Lakṣmaṇa, who could withstand him, blazing like a fire fanned by the wind?
t.5.35.67: O chief of the monkeys, who could withstand in battle Rāghava together with Lakṣmaṇa, that crusher of foes in combat, standing firm like a maddened elephant of the quarters, like the sun at the end of the age, with arrows for his blazing rays?
t.5.35.68: Therefore, O best of monkeys, quickly bring my husband here together with Lakṣmaṇa and the troop-leaders; O chief of the monkeys, make me joyful, I who have long been wasted by grief for Rāma.
